questions.title: Best description of the Golgi tendon organs
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Golgi tendon organs?

options.A: They are located in parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers
options.B: They are inhibited when the muscle actively contracts
options.C: They are the receptors for the inverse stretch reflex
options.D: They are connected to group Ia afferent fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. Golgi tendon organs lie in SERIES (at the musculotendinous junction), not in parallel; the in-parallel receptors are the muscle spindles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. They are ACTIVATED (excited) by active contraction because it raises tendon tension; they are not inhibited by it.
explanations.C: Correct. Golgi tendon organs are tension receptors in series with the muscle fibres, and their group Ib afferents drive the inverse (autogenic) stretch reflex. Through an inhibitory interneuron they inhibit the homonymous alpha motor neurons, so a steep rise in tension makes the contracting muscle relax. This protects the muscle-tendon unit from excessive force and helps grade contraction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Golgi tendon organs are connected to group Ib afferents; the group Ia afferents belong to the muscle spindle's primary ending.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi tendon organ as the in-series tension receptor (Ib afferent) of the inhibitory inverse stretch reflex.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Control > Golgi Tendon Organ

questions.title: Bladder during spinal shock
questions.question: Which of the following describes the urinary bladder of a patient during the stage of spinal shock?

options.B: Automatic bladder
options.C: Hyperactive bladder with mass reflex
options.D: Evacuated only by voluntary control

explanations.A: Correct. During spinal shock all reflexes below a sudden complete cord transection are abolished, so the detrusor is atonic (areflexic). The bladder therefore fills passively and cannot empty, producing urinary retention, and once over-full it dribbles out passively as retention with overflow. Only when reflexes later return does an automatic bladder develop.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The automatic (reflex) bladder appears in the RECOVERY stage after spinal shock, not during it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A hyperactive bladder with mass reflex is also a late, post-shock recovery pattern, not a feature of spinal shock.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Voluntary control requires intact descending pathways, which are lost below a complete transection; the shock-stage bladder cannot be voluntarily emptied.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the atonic, retention-with-overflow bladder of spinal shock versus the later automatic bladder.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Spinal Cord > Spinal Shock

questions.title: Cord level whose transection causes immediate death
questions.question: Lesion at which level of the spinal cord causes immediate death?

options.A: Transection at the upper cervical level
options.B: Transection at lower cervical level
options.C: Transection in the upper thoracic region
options.D: Transection in the lower lumbar region

explanations.A: Correct. The phrenic nerve to the diaphragm arises from C3-C5 and the intercostal nerves from the thoracic segments. A transection above this level (upper cervical) cuts descending drive to both the phrenic and intercostal motor neurons, paralysing all the respiratory muscles, so death from respiratory arrest is immediate unless the patient is ventilated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A lower cervical lesion can spare the phrenic outflow, preserving diaphragmatic breathing, so it is not immediately fatal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An upper thoracic lesion leaves diaphragmatic (phrenic) breathing intact and is not immediately fatal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A lower lumbar lesion is well below the respiratory outflow and does not threaten breathing.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why an upper-cervical cord transection above the phrenic origin is immediately fatal.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Spinal Cord > Cord Transection Levels

questions.title: Hair cells of the crista ampullaris
questions.question: Which statement concerning the hair cells of the crista ampullaris is correct?

options.A: Movement that bends the stereocilia towards the kinocilium depolarizes the hair cell
options.B: Bending of the stereocilia to the kinocilium activates voltage-gated sodium channels
options.C: Depolarization of the hair cell is achieved by linear acceleration
options.D: They are stimulated with constant speed rotation

explanations.A: Correct. Each hair cell has a bundle of stereocilia and one tall kinocilium. Deflection of the stereocilia TOWARD the kinocilium opens mechanically-gated cation channels and admits K+ from the surrounding endolymph, depolarising the cell and increasing afferent firing; bending away hyperpolarises it. This directional sensitivity lets the crista signal the direction of angular acceleration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transduction opens mechanically-gated cation channels carrying a K+ current from endolymph, not voltage-gated sodium channels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The crista responds to ANGULAR acceleration; linear acceleration is detected by the maculae of the utricle and saccule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cristae respond to CHANGES in rotation (angular acceleration/deceleration); at constant speed rotation the endolymph catches up and the cupula returns, so firing subsides.

questions.learning_objective: State that stereocilia deflection toward the kinocilium depolarises the vestibular hair cell via K+ influx from endolymph.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Vestibular Hair Cell

questions.title: Structure sensitive to vertical linear head movement
questions.question: Which of the following structures is maximally sensitive to linear head movement in the vertical plane?

options.B: Macula of the saccule
options.C: Crista ampullaris of the anterior semicircular duct
options.D: Crista ampullaris of the horizontal semicircular duct

explanations.A: Incorrect. The utricular macula lies in the HORIZONTAL plane and detects horizontal linear acceleration and head tilt, not vertical movement.
explanations.B: Correct. The otolith organs sense linear acceleration through a CaCO3-loaded otolithic membrane. The macula of the SACCULE is oriented in the vertical (sagittal) plane, so it is maximally sensitive to vertical linear movement (e.g. riding a lift) and to the pull of gravity along that axis, whereas the utricular macula covers the horizontal plane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A crista ampullaris detects ANGULAR (rotational) acceleration, not linear movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The horizontal semicircular duct's crista detects rotation in the horizontal plane (angular acceleration), not vertical linear movement.

questions.learning_objective: Assign vertical-plane linear acceleration to the saccular macula, contrasting it with the utricle and the cristae.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Otolith Organs

questions.title: The premotor cortex
questions.question: Which statement concerning the premotor cortex is correct?

options.A: It is located just posterior to the primary motor cortex
options.B: It is facilitatory to muscle tone
options.C: It controls pattern of complex coordinated gross movements
options.D: It contains highly excitable Betz cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. The premotor cortex (area 6) lies just ANTERIOR to the primary motor cortex, not posterior (the postcentral gyrus behind it is sensory).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Its role is programming movement patterns, not simple facilitation of muscle tone.
explanations.C: Correct. The premotor cortex organises learned, coordinated patterns of complex gross movement — sequences and postural sets involving many muscle groups — which it feeds forward to the primary motor cortex for execution, working with the supplementary motor area and basal ganglia in planning. It is concerned with movement patterning rather than with generating the final descending command.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The giant Betz cells are in the PRIMARY motor cortex (area 4), not the premotor cortex.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the premotor cortex as programming complex coordinated gross-movement patterns anterior to area 4.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Cortex > Premotor Area

questions.title: Area damaged in effortful non-fluent speech
questions.question: A person who has had a traumatic brain injury seems to be able to understand the written and spoken word but his speech is poorly articulated, produced slowly and with great effort. This person most likely has damage to which area of the brain?

options.B: Broca's area
options.C: Angular gyrus
options.D: Auditory association area

explanations.A: Incorrect. A Wernicke's-area lesion gives FLUENT speech with impaired comprehension, the opposite of this patient's preserved understanding with effortful output.
explanations.B: Correct. Broca's area (areas 44, 45) in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus programmes the motor sequences of speech, so its lesion causes an expressive (motor, non-fluent) aphasia: the patient understands language but speaks slowly, effortfully and with poor articulation. Comprehension is preserved because Wernicke's sensory area is intact. Good comprehension with laboured output localises to Broca's area.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The angular gyrus is involved in reading/writing and cross-modal association; its lesion does not produce this effortful, non-fluent articulation pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The auditory association area processes complex sounds; its lesion does not cause non-fluent expressive aphasia.

questions.learning_objective: Localise effortful, poorly articulated speech with intact comprehension to a Broca's-area lesion.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Language > Broca's Area

questions.title: Condition showing hypertonia and hyperreflexia
questions.question: Hypertonia and hyperreflexia are shown in which of the following conditions?

options.B: Sleep
options.C: Lower motor neuron lesion
options.D: Upper motor neuron lesion

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypothyroidism classically slows the reflexes (delayed relaxation, hyporeflexia), not hyperreflexia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscle tone and reflex activity are reduced during sleep, not exaggerated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A lower motor neuron lesion gives HYPOtonia and HYPOreflexia (with wasting and fasciculation), the opposite of this picture.
explanations.D: Correct. An upper motor neuron lesion removes descending cortical inhibition of the spinal reflex arcs, so muscle tone rises (spastic hypertonia) and the deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated (hyperreflexia), often with clonus and an extensor plantar. These 'release' signs are the hallmark of a UMN lesion.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute hypertonia and hyperreflexia to an upper motor neuron (release) lesion.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Lesions > Upper Motor Neuron

questions.title: Feature of lower motor neuron disease
questions.question: In lower motor neuron disease, the subject may show:

options.B: Hyperactive reflexes
options.C: Wasting of muscles
options.D: Clonus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rigidity/spastic hypertonia is an UPPER motor neuron (or basal-ganglia) feature; an LMN lesion gives flaccidity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reflexes are DEPRESSED or absent in an LMN lesion, not hyperactive.
explanations.C: Correct. A lower motor neuron lesion interrupts the final common path to the muscle, denervating it. The denervated muscle undergoes marked WASTING (atrophy) together with fasciculations and, on EMG, fibrillations, and becomes flaccid with absent reflexes. Muscle wasting with fasciculation is the hallmark of denervation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Clonus is a sign of exaggerated stretch reflexes and belongs to UPPER motor neuron lesions, not LMN disease.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise muscle wasting as a lower-motor-neuron (denervation) sign.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Lesions > Lower Motor Neuron

questions.title: Manifestation of upper motor neuron lesion
questions.question: Upper motor neuron lesion is manifested by:

options.B: Muscle wasting
options.C: Normal planter response
options.D: Fasciculation

explanations.A: Correct. An upper motor neuron lesion produces a SPASTIC paralysis: loss of descending inhibition raises tone (clasp-knife hypertonia) with hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar. Paralysis affects muscle groups rather than single muscles, with little wasting and no fasciculation. Spastic paralysis is the defining UMN manifestation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Marked muscle wasting is a LOWER motor neuron (denervation) feature; UMN lesions show only mild disuse atrophy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A UMN lesion gives an ABNORMAL (extensor, Babinski) plantar response, not a normal flexor one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fasciculations reflect denervation and are LOWER motor neuron signs, not UMN signs.

questions.learning_objective: Identify spastic paralysis as the manifestation of an upper motor neuron lesion.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Lesions > Upper Motor Neuron

questions.title: Symptom of Parkinsonism
questions.question: Which of the following is a symptom of Parkinsonism?

options.B: High steppage gait
options.C: Slow monotonous speech
options.D: Hypotonia

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Parkinsonian tremor is a RESTING (pill-rolling) tremor; a kinetic (intention) tremor is a cerebellar sign.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A high-steppage gait indicates foot drop or sensory ataxia; Parkinsonism gives a shuffling, festinant gait.
explanations.C: Correct. Parkinsonism (nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration) produces a hypokinetic dysarthria — speech that is slow, soft and MONOTONOUS — alongside the triad of resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia. Slow monotonous speech is therefore a recognised Parkinsonian sign.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tone is INCREASED (lead-pipe/cogwheel rigidity) in Parkinsonism, so hypotonia is not a feature.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise slow monotonous speech (with resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia) as a Parkinsonian feature.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Basal Ganglia > Parkinsonism

questions.title: General functional role of the cerebellum
questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning the general functional role of the cerebellum is correct?

options.A: The cerebellum directly stimulates motor neurons required to make a movement
options.B: The cerebellum controls muscle activity on the opposite side of the body
options.C: The cerebellum plays an active role in the coordination of the muscles required to make a movement
options.D: The cerebellum is not involved in the planning of a movement, only its execution

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cerebellum does not directly drive lower motor neurons; it modulates and coordinates the motor command generated elsewhere.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cerebellum acts on the SAME (ipsilateral) side of the body, because its output crosses and the corticospinal tract crosses again (double crossing).
explanations.C: Correct. The cerebellum compares the intended movement with the actual movement using proprioceptive feedback and issues corrective signals that coordinate the timing, force and sequence of the muscles involved. Its overall role is coordination, so its disease produces incoordination (ataxia) rather than paralysis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cerebellum participates in the PLANNING of movement (via its lateral zone and cortical connections) as well as its smooth execution.

questions.learning_objective: State the cerebellum's role as ipsilateral coordination (and planning) of movement, not direct motor-neuron drive.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Cerebellum > General Function

questions.title: Functional role of the cerebellar intermediate zone
questions.question: Which of the following statements best describes a functional role for the intermediate zone of the cerebellum?

options.B: Servo comparator function and sends corrective impulses to the cortex
options.C: Planning function through connection with the cerebral cortex
options.D: Functions with the vestibular nucleus to control equilibrium

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple facilitation of muscle tone is not the defining role of the intermediate zone; that is more a vermal/vestibular function.
explanations.B: Correct. The intermediate (paravermal) zone receives both the motor command (a corollary discharge from the cortex) and sensory feedback about the limb's actual movement. It therefore works as a servo-comparator, detecting the error between the intended and the actual movement. It then sends corrective impulses back through the interposed nuclei and thalamus to the cortex, and via the red nucleus, to smooth the ongoing limb movement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The PLANNING function through cortical connections belongs to the LATERAL cerebellar zone, not the intermediate zone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Equilibrium control with the vestibular nuclei is the role of the flocculonodular lobe/vermis, not the intermediate zone.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the cerebellar intermediate zone as a servo-comparator returning corrective impulses.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Cerebellum > Functional Zones

questions.title: Symptom type produced by cerebellar disease
questions.question: Neurological disease associated with the cerebellum produces which of the following types of symptoms?

options.B: Akinesia
options.C: Rigidity
options.D: Ataxia

explanations.A: Incorrect. A resting tremor is a basal-ganglia (Parkinsonian) sign; the cerebellar tremor is an intention (kinetic) tremor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Akinesia/bradykinesia is a basal-ganglia feature, not a cerebellar one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rigidity is a basal-ganglia sign; cerebellar disease causes HYPOtonia.
explanations.D: Correct. Because the cerebellum coordinates movement, its disease produces incoordination — ataxia — with a broad-based staggering gait, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, an intention tremor, scanning speech, nystagmus and hypotonia, all ipsilateral to the lesion. Ataxia is the unifying cerebellar sign.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ataxia as the hallmark of cerebellar disease, distinct from Parkinsonian signs.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Cerebellum > Cerebellar Signs

questions.title: Correct statement on EEG activity
questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning electroencephalogram activity is correct?

options.A: Beta waves occur in normal adults who are awake but in a quiet, resting state
options.B: Alpha waves occur during periods of increased brain activity and thinking
options.C: Theta waves are recorded during REM sleep
options.D: Delta waves are characteristic of slow wave sleep

explanations.A: Incorrect. The awake, quiet, relaxed (eyes-closed) adult shows ALPHA waves; beta waves appear with alertness and mental activity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased brain activity and thinking produce BETA waves, not alpha.
explanations.C: Incorrect. REM sleep shows a desynchronised, low-voltage fast (awake-like) EEG; theta waves are typical of drowsiness/children rather than REM.
explanations.D: Correct. Delta waves (below 4 Hz, high amplitude) dominate deep slow-wave (stage 3-4 NREM) sleep. They are the slowest, largest EEG rhythm and, appearing in a waking adult, would suggest organic brain disease. Delta with slow-wave sleep is the correct pairing.

questions.learning_objective: Pair delta waves with slow-wave sleep and place alpha, beta and theta correctly.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > EEG and Sleep > EEG Rhythms

questions.title: Characteristic finding in REM sleep
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in REM sleep phase?

options.B: Increase heart rate and respiratory rate
options.C: The eyes are deviated up
options.D: Dreams which are not remembered

explanations.A: Incorrect. REM sleep ABOLISHES skeletal muscle tone (atonia) except for the eye and respiratory muscles; tone is not increased.
explanations.B: Correct. REM (paradoxical) sleep is a state of autonomic activation: heart rate and respiratory rate RISE and fluctuate and blood pressure varies, alongside a desynchronised awake-like EEG, rapid conjugate eye movements and muscle atonia. Increased, irregular heart and respiratory rate is the characteristic REM feature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. REM is defined by rapid conjugate eye MOVEMENTS in various directions, not a sustained upward deviation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dreams during REM are typically vivid and REMEMBERED if the sleeper wakes from that stage.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise raised, irregular heart and respiratory rate (with atonia and recalled dreams) as REM features.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > EEG and Sleep > REM Sleep

questions.title: Cause of blindness from pressure on the optic nerve
questions.question: Which of the following is a major cause of blindness due to increased pressure on the optic nerve?

options.B: Astigmatism
options.C: Glaucoma
options.D: Presbyopia

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cataract is an opacity of the lens; it blocks light rather than raising pressure on the optic nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Astigmatism is an irregular corneal/lens curvature causing blurred focus, not raised intraocular pressure.
explanations.C: Correct. Glaucoma is a raised intraocular pressure from impaired aqueous drainage (trabecular meshwork/canal of Schlemm). The sustained high pressure compresses the optic nerve head and its blood supply, progressively destroying retinal ganglion-cell axons and causing an irreversible, characteristically peripheral-first field loss that can end in blindness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation from a stiffening lens; it does not raise optic-nerve pressure.

questions.learning_objective: Explain glaucoma as raised intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Glaucoma

questions.title: Causes of corneal transparency EXCEPT
questions.question: All of the following are causes of corneal transparency Except:

options.B: It is avascular
options.C: Relative corneal dehydration
options.D: It is supplied by myelinated sensory nerve fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a cause). A non-keratinised surface epithelium keeps the cornea smooth and clear, contributing to transparency.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a cause). The avascular stroma has no blood vessels to scatter light, a key basis of transparency.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a cause). Relative corneal dehydration, maintained by the endothelial pump, prevents light-scattering oedema.
explanations.D: Correct (this is the EXCEPTION). Corneal sensory nerves lose their myelin sheaths soon after entering the cornea, because myelin would scatter light; the cornea is therefore supplied by NON-myelinated nerve fibres centrally. A supply of myelinated fibres would not aid transparency, making this the odd one out.

questions.learning_objective: List the determinants of corneal transparency and identify myelinated nerves as NOT a cause.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Corneal Transparency

questions.title: Basis of the fovea's high visual acuity
questions.question: The fovea centralis has the highest visual acuity because:

options.B: Rods are covered by blood vessels
options.C: Absence of convergence on the bipolar cells
options.D: The pigmented epithelium of fovea is not well developed

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fovea is packed with CONES, not rods; rods are absent at the foveal centre.
explanations.B: Incorrect. At the foveal pit the inner layers and blood vessels are swept ASIDE so light reaches the cones directly; photoreceptors are not covered by vessels.
explanations.C: Correct. Each foveal cone connects essentially one-to-one through a single midget bipolar cell to a single ganglion cell, so there is little or no convergence. This preserves fine spatial detail and gives the fovea the highest acuity, whereas the peripheral rod system has high convergence favouring sensitivity over acuity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pigment epithelium is present and functional at the fovea; foveal acuity comes from the one-to-one cone wiring, not from poorly developed pigment epithelium.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute foveal acuity to minimal convergence (near one-to-one cone-bipolar-ganglion wiring).
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Foveal Acuity

questions.title: Feature of dark adaptation
questions.question: In dark adaptation:

options.B: Decreased signal intensity in retinal neurons
options.C: Constriction of pupils
options.D: Retinal threshold increase

explanations.A: Correct. Dark adaptation is the progressive INCREASE in retinal sensitivity that occurs on moving into darkness. In the dark, bleached photopigments (rhodopsin in rods, and cone pigments) regenerate, so the threshold for detecting light falls and dim signals are amplified; the cone limb adapts within minutes and the more sensitive rod limb over 20-30 minutes. Increased sensitivity (lowered threshold) is the essence of dark adaptation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Signal intensity for a given dim light INCREASES as sensitivity rises, not decreases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pupils DILATE in the dark to admit more light, not constrict.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The retinal threshold FALLS (the retina becomes more sensitive) during dark adaptation, so a rising threshold is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Define dark adaptation as increased retinal sensitivity (lowered threshold) with pupillary dilatation.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Dark Adaptation

questions.title: Event that makes a sound interpreted as loud
questions.question: Which of the following events makes the auditory system interpret a sound as loud?

options.A: Fewer inner hair cells are stimulated
options.B: Hair cells excite nerve endings at a diminished rate
options.C: Amplitude of vibration of the basilar membrane decreases
options.D: Amplitude of vibration of the basilar membrane increases

explanations.A: Incorrect. A loud sound recruits MORE hair cells over a wider area of membrane, not fewer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Loudness raises the firing rate of the auditory afferents; a diminished rate signals a softer sound.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decreased vibration amplitude means less stimulation and a softer, not louder, sound.
explanations.D: Correct. A louder sound produces a larger-amplitude vibration of the basilar membrane, which bends more hair-cell stereocilia more strongly. This increases afferent firing rate AND recruits more hair cells, so the auditory system interprets the sound as loud through greater neural activity. (Pitch, by contrast, is coded by the place of maximal vibration.)

questions.learning_objective: Attribute perceived loudness to increased basilar-membrane vibration amplitude, higher firing and more hair cells.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Loudness Coding

questions.title: Statement regarding hair cells
questions.question: Regarding hair cells:

options.A: Hair cells depolarize when their hairs are bent toward the modiolus
options.B: Nerve fibers stimulated by hair cells have their cell bodies in the cochlear nuclei of the brain stem
options.C: There are more inner hair cells than outer hair cells in the organ of corti
options.D: Transmission of auditory signals is performed mainly by inner hair cells than outer hair cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cochlear hair cells depolarise when their stereocilia bend AWAY from the modiolus (toward the tallest row/stria), not toward the modiolus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The afferent fibres stimulated by the hair cells have their cell bodies in the SPIRAL (cochlear) GANGLION, not in the brainstem cochlear nuclei.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is one row of inner hair cells and three rows of outer hair cells, so outer hair cells are MORE numerous.
explanations.D: Correct. Although outer hair cells outnumber inner ones, transmission of auditory information to the brain is performed MAINLY by the inner hair cells. The inner hair cells receive about 90-95% of the afferent (type I) fibres of the cochlear nerve. The outer hair cells instead act chiefly as a cochlear amplifier through their electromotility.

questions.learning_objective: State that inner hair cells carry most auditory afferent signalling, with cell bodies in the spiral ganglion.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Cochlear Hair Cells

questions.title: Amplification of sound by the middle ear
questions.question: Amplification of sound by the middle ear:

options.A: Occurs because the ligaments connecting the bones are usually flexible
options.B: Is decreased by cutting the facial nerve
options.C: Is caused by the fact that the tympanic membrane is larger in area than the oval window
options.D: Occurs because the ossicles act as a lever system to increase the sound 12 times

explanations.A: Incorrect. Efficient transfer needs RIGID ossicular coupling; flexible ligaments would waste energy, not amplify.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cutting the facial nerve paralyses stapedius and REMOVES its dampening reflex, so if anything transmission of loud sound increases; it does not decrease amplification.
explanations.C: Correct. The middle ear matches air to cochlear-fluid impedance mainly through the AREA RATIO: the large tympanic membrane collects sound force and concentrates it onto the much smaller stapes footplate/oval window, raising pressure roughly 17-fold. This area ratio is the dominant amplifying mechanism, with the ossicular lever adding a smaller factor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ossicular lever contributes only a small factor (about 1.3x), not a 12-fold gain; the main amplification is the area ratio.

questions.learning_objective: Explain middle-ear amplification chiefly by the tympanic-to-oval-window area ratio.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Middle Ear Amplification

questions.title: Effect of vitamin A deficiency
questions.question: Vitamin A deficiency causes:

options.B: Poor color vision
options.C: Astigmatism
options.D: Presbyopia

explanations.A: Correct. Vitamin A (retinol) is the precursor of 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin in rods. In deficiency, rhodopsin cannot be regenerated fast enough, so rod (dim-light) vision fails first and the earliest symptom is night blindness (nyctalopia). Prolonged deficiency also causes conjunctival/corneal xerosis and keratomalacia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Colour vision is a CONE function and is relatively preserved early; the rod-dependent night vision fails first.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Astigmatism is an irregular corneal/lens curvature, unrelated to vitamin A.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation, not a vitamin A deficiency effect.

questions.learning_objective: Link vitamin A deficiency to night blindness through impaired rhodopsin regeneration.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Special Senses > Vitamin A and Vision

questions.title: Site of unmyelinated fibres with Schwann cells
questions.question: Unmyelinated nerve fibres with Schwann cells are found in:

options.B: Post ganglionic sympathetic fibers
options.C: Grey matter
options.D: White matter

explanations.A: Incorrect as the best answer. 'Peripheral nerve fibers' is too broad — many are myelinated; the question asks specifically where unmyelinated Schwann-invested fibres are found.
explanations.B: Correct. Even unmyelinated peripheral axons are cradled in grooves of Schwann cells (Remak bundles) without a spiral myelin wrapping. The small, slow POSTGANGLIONIC SYMPATHETIC (autonomic) fibres — like C pain fibres — are the classic example of unmyelinated fibres ensheathed by Schwann cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CNS grey matter contains unmyelinated axons too, but they are supported by glia (astrocytes/oligodendrocytes), NOT Schwann cells, which are peripheral.
explanations.D: Incorrect. White matter axons are central and myelinated by oligodendrocytes; Schwann cells are not present in the CNS.

questions.learning_objective: Identify postganglionic sympathetic fibres as peripheral unmyelinated axons ensheathed by Schwann cells.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Peripheral Nerve > Unmyelinated Fibres

questions.title: Cell type of the cerebellar Purkinje cell
questions.question: Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex are an example of:

options.B: Multipolar pyramidal nerve cell
options.C: Unipolar nerve cell
options.D: Multipolar pyriform nerve cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bipolar neurons (e.g. retinal bipolar cells, olfactory receptors) have two processes; the Purkinje cell has one axon and an elaborate dendritic tree (multipolar).
explanations.B: Incorrect. 'Pyramidal' cells belong to the cerebral cortex/hippocampus; the Purkinje cell is pyriform, not pyramidal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons are sensory ganglion cells; the Purkinje cell is multipolar.
explanations.D: Correct. Purkinje cells are large MULTIPOLAR neurons with a distinctive flask-shaped (PYRIFORM) cell body, arranged in a single row, giving off one elaborate planar dendritic tree into the molecular layer and a single axon to the deep cerebellar nuclei. Multipolar pyriform is the defining Purkinje morphology.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the Purkinje cell as a large multipolar neuron with a pyriform body.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Cerebellar Cortex > Purkinje Cell

questions.title: Statement that best applies to neuroglia
questions.question: The answer that best applies to neuroglia is:

options.A: Spines decorate cell body & branches of mesoglia
options.B: Protoplasmic astrocytes have few long processes
options.C: Microglia have centrioles, so can divide
options.D: Ependymal cells are found around nerve cells in ganglia

explanations.A: Correct. Microglia (mesoglia) are the small phagocytic glia of the CNS, and their short branching processes — and the cell body — are covered with fine SPINE-LIKE (thorny) projections. This spiny appearance decorating the cell body and branches identifies the mesoglia/microglia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protoplasmic astrocytes (grey matter) have MANY SHORT branching processes; it is the fibrous astrocytes (white matter) that have fewer, longer processes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Microglia are of mesodermal (monocyte) origin and are not characterised by centriole-driven mitosis in this scheme; they proliferate mainly by recruitment in injury.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cells surrounding neurons in ganglia are SATELLITE cells; ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal.

questions.learning_objective: Identify microglia (mesoglia) by their small size and short spiny processes.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Neuroglia > Microglia

questions.title: True statement about nerve endings
questions.question: Regarding the nerve endings, which of the following statements is true?

options.A: Free nerve endings in C.T. are mechanoreceptors for movement & position
options.B: In tendon spindle, sensory nerve ends around the collagen bundles
options.C: Intrafusal fibers have central striated area with no nuclei
options.D: Ruffini corpuscles are nerve endings in muscular tissue

explanations.A: Incorrect. Free nerve endings mainly signal pain and temperature (and crude touch); movement and position sense are served by encapsulated/proprioceptive endings, not free endings.
explanations.B: Correct. The tendon spindle (Golgi tendon organ) has its sensory (Ib) nerve ending winding around and interdigitating with the collagen fibre bundles of the tendon, so it is stimulated by the tension those bundles transmit during muscle contraction. This wrapping around collagen bundles is the defining structural feature of the tendon organ.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The central (equatorial) region of an intrafusal fibre is NON-striated and NUCLEATED (nuclear bag or chain); it is not a striated, nucleus-free area.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ruffini corpuscles are slowly-adapting mechanoreceptors of the DERMIS/connective tissue (skin and joint capsules), not endings within muscular tissue.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi tendon organ's sensory ending winding around tendon collagen bundles.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Nerve Endings > Golgi Tendon Organ

questions.title: Correct statement on the vestibular apparatus
questions.question: At view of the vestibular apparatus, which statement is correct?

options.A: Cristae ampullaris register vertical acceleration & deceleration of the head
options.B: Utricle & saccule are membranous sacs lined by simple columnar epithelium
options.C: Columnar supporting cells have apical stereocilia
options.D: Cells of cristae ampullaris are covered by (cupula) that lacks CaCO3 crystals

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cristae register ANGULAR (rotational) acceleration; linear vertical acceleration is sensed by the maculae (saccule).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sensory maculae are lined by a specialised neuroepithelium of hair cells and supporting cells, not a simple columnar epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stereocilia are the apical specialisation of the HAIR (sensory) cells, not of the supporting cells.
explanations.D: Correct. The crista ampullaris is capped by the cupula, a dome of gelatinous proteoglycan embedding the hair-cell stereocilia. Unlike the otolithic membrane of the maculae, the cupula contains NO calcium carbonate (CaCO3) otoliths, so it is not weighted by gravity and is deflected by endolymph movement during angular acceleration.

questions.learning_objective: State that the crista's cupula lacks CaCO3 otoliths, making it an angular-acceleration detector.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Vestibular Apparatus > Crista Ampullaris

questions.title: Structure formed by Reissner's membrane
questions.question: Reissner's (vestibular) membrane forms the:

options.A: Outer wall of the cochlear duct
options.B: Roof of the cochlear duct
options.C: Floor of the cochlear duct
options.D: Spiral lamina

explanations.A: Incorrect. The OUTER WALL of the cochlear duct is the stria vascularis, not Reissner's membrane.
explanations.B: Correct. The cochlear duct (scala media) is triangular: Reissner's (vestibular) membrane forms its ROOF, separating the endolymph of the duct from the perilymph of the scala vestibuli above. It is a thin, two-cell-layered partition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The FLOOR of the cochlear duct is the basilar membrane, which bears the organ of Corti, not Reissner's membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spiral (osseous) lamina is a bony shelf projecting from the modiolus; it is not formed by Reissner's membrane.

questions.learning_objective: Locate Reissner's membrane as the roof of the cochlear duct.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Cochlea > Cochlear Duct

questions.title: Correct statement regarding retinal rod cells
questions.question: In retina, which of the following is correct regarding the rod cells?

options.A: Its inner fiber ends by a pedicle
options.B: Its discs are continuously shed off and phagocytosed
options.C: Located mainly at the center of retina
options.D: Slight constriction between inner segment and cell body

explanations.A: Incorrect. The rod's inner fibre ends in a small SPHERULE; the flat PEDICLE is the synaptic ending of the CONE, not the rod.
explanations.B: Correct. A rod's outer segment is a stack of rhodopsin-laden membranous discs that are continuously renewed: new discs form at the base while the oldest discs at the tip are SHED and PHAGOCYTOSED by the adjacent retinal pigment epithelium, which recycles their components. Continuous disc shedding and phagocytosis is the defining feature of the rod outer segment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rods are concentrated in the PERIPHERAL retina; the central fovea is cone-rich and rod-free.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The characteristic narrowing in a photoreceptor is the connecting cilium between the OUTER and inner segments, not a constriction between inner segment and cell body.

questions.learning_objective: Describe continuous shedding of rod outer-segment discs and their phagocytosis by the pigment epithelium.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Retina > Rod Cell

questions.title: Why a corneal graft is not rejected
questions.question: After corneal transplantation, which structural feature best explains why the corneal graft is not rejected by the recipient?

options.A: Basal cells of the corneal epithelium are able to regenerate
options.B: The Bowman membrane protects against the spread of infections
options.C: Collagen fibres are regularly packed
options.D: The cornea is avascular and lacks lymphatic drainage

explanations.A: Incorrect. The regenerative capacity of the basal epithelial cells explains rapid re-epithelialisation and healing, not immune tolerance of the graft.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bowman's membrane is an acellular barrier layer; it plays no role in preventing graft rejection, which is an immunological event.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The regular, uniform packing of stromal collagen lamellae explains corneal transparency, not immune privilege.
explanations.D: Correct. The cornea is avascular and has no lymphatic drainage, so donor antigens cannot be efficiently carried to regional lymph nodes (afferent arm) and host effector cells and antibodies cannot readily reach the graft (efferent arm). This anatomical isolation is the basis of corneal immune privilege, which is why corneal allografts are accepted far more often than vascularised-tissue grafts.

questions.learning_objective: Explain corneal graft acceptance by the cornea's avascularity and lack of lymphatic drainage.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Eye > Cornea

questions.title: Histology of the corneal epithelium
questions.question: Microscopic examination of the corneal epithelium reveals that:

options.B: It is a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
options.C: It contains many myelinated nerve fibres
options.D: It shows few mitotic figures

explanations.A: Correct. The corneal epithelium is a non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium whose superficial squamous cells bear surface microvilli (and microplicae). These project into the tear film and help anchor and stabilise it over the avascular cornea.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The corneal epithelium is NON-keratinized; a keratinized surface would be opaque and is not found on the normal cornea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cornea is richly innervated, but by free, NON-myelinated sensory nerve endings; myelinated fibres lose their myelin on entering the cornea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epithelium is highly mitotically active with frequent basal-layer mitoses, giving it rapid turnover and strong regenerative capacity — not few mitotic figures.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise surface microvilli on the non-keratinized corneal epithelium.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Eye > Cornea

questions.title: Histology of the iris
questions.question: Concerning the iris, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Its stroma is formed of loose vascular pigmented connective tissue
options.B: Fibroblasts and melanocytes cover its posterior surface
options.C: Pigmented epithelium covers its anterior surface
options.D: It is the posterior part of the vascular coat

explanations.A: Correct. The iris stroma is loose, vascular, pigmented connective tissue containing melanocytes, fibroblasts, blood vessels and the sphincter and dilator pupillae smooth muscles. Its melanocyte content is what determines eye colour.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the ANTERIOR surface of the iris that is covered by a discontinuous layer of fibroblasts and melanocytes; the posterior surface carries pigmented epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pigmented (two-layered) epithelium covers the POSTERIOR surface of the iris, not the anterior surface.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The iris is the most ANTERIOR part of the vascular (uveal) coat; the choroid is its posterior part.

questions.learning_objective: State that the iris stroma is loose vascular pigmented CT and place the iris as the anterior uveal coat.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Histology > Eye > Iris
